Linear Algebra — 02 · Vector Spaces, Subspaces, Basis and Dimension

Created2025-05-26|Updated2025-05-26|Mathematics > Linear Algebra
|Post View:

Linear Algebra 00 and 01 worked with columns of numbers. This post asks what those columns have in common with polynomials, functions, matrices and the solutions of a differential equation — and answers with one definition: a vector space. From that definition come the ideas that organise the rest of the subject: subspaces, span, linear independence, basis and dimension. The central theorem is that dimension is well defined — every basis of a space has the same size — and it is proved here in full through the Steinitz exchange lemma. The abstract ideas are then brought back to matrices through Strang's four fundamental subspaces, with a complete worked example, a proof that row rank equals column rank, and the rank–nullity theorem in matrix form. The post ends with sums and direct sums of subspaces and the formula dim⁡(U+W)=dim⁡U+dim⁡W−dim⁡(U∩W)\dim(U + W) = \dim U + \dim W - \dim(U \cap W)dim(U+W)=dimU+dimW−dim(U∩W).

Series map: 00 Vectors & Linear Systems → 01 Matrix Algebra, Inverses & LU → 02 Vector Spaces, Basis & Dimension (this post) → 03 Linear Maps, Change of Basis & Determinants → 04 Eigenvalues & Diagonalization → 05 Inner Products, Spectral Theorem & SVD.

Learning Outcome

  • State the axioms of a vector space over a field, and check them for FnF^nFn, polynomials, functions and matrices.
  • Prove simple consequences of the axioms, such as 0v=00\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}0v=0 and (−1)v=−v(-1)\mathbf{v} = -\mathbf{v}(−1)v=−v.
  • Use the subspace test, and recognise common subspaces and non-subspaces.
  • Work with span and linear independence in any vector space, including the linear dependence lemma.
  • Prove the Steinitz exchange lemma and deduce that dimension is well defined.
  • Extend an independent list to a basis, shrink a spanning list to a basis, and compute coordinates.
  • Find bases and dimensions of the four fundamental subspaces of a matrix from its RREF.
  • Prove that row rank equals column rank and that rank⁡A+dim⁡N(A)=n\operatorname{rank} A + \dim N(A) = nrankA+dimN(A)=n.
  • Work with sums and direct sums, and prove the dimension formula for U+WU + WU+W.

Chapter 1 — Fields and vector spaces

Terminology

  • Field — a set FFF with an addition and a multiplication that satisfy the usual rules of arithmetic: both operations are associative and commutative, multiplication distributes over addition, there are elements 0≠10 \neq 10=1 with a+0=aa + 0 = aa+0=a and 1a=a1a = a1a=a, every aaa has a negative −a-a−a, and every nonzero aaa has an inverse a−1a^{-1}a−1. Examples: Q\mathbb{Q}Q, R\mathbb{R}R, C\mathbb{C}C, and F2={0,1}\mathbb{F}_2 = \{0, 1\}F2​={0,1} with arithmetic mod 2. The integers Z\mathbb{Z}Z are not a field (222 has no integer inverse).
  • Scalars — the elements of the field. In this series FFF is R\mathbb{R}R or C\mathbb{C}C unless stated.

Everything in Linear Algebra 00 and 01 — elimination, pivots, inverses, LU — used only these field rules, so it works word for word over any field.

The definition

A vector space over FFF is a set VVV with an addition V×V→VV \times V \to VV×V→V and a scalar multiplication F×V→VF \times V \to VF×V→V such that, for all u,v,w∈V\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{w} \in Vu,v,w∈V and a,b∈Fa, b \in Fa,b∈F:

  1. u+v=v+u\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v} + \mathbf{u}u+v=v+u (commutativity).
  2. (u+v)+w=u+(v+w)(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}) + \mathbf{w} = \mathbf{u} + (\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{w})(u+v)+w=u+(v+w) (associativity).
  3. There is an element 0∈V\mathbf{0} \in V0∈V with v+0=v\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{0} = \mathbf{v}v+0=v for all v\mathbf{v}v (additive identity).
  4. For each v\mathbf{v}v there is w\mathbf{w}w with v+w=0\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{w} = \mathbf{0}v+w=0 (additive inverse).
  5. a(bv)=(ab)va(b\mathbf{v}) = (ab)\mathbf{v}a(bv)=(ab)v.
  6. 1v=v1\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v}1v=v.
  7. a(u+v)=au+ava(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}) = a\mathbf{u} + a\mathbf{v}a(u+v)=au+av.
  8. (a+b)v=av+bv(a + b)\mathbf{v} = a\mathbf{v} + b\mathbf{v}(a+b)v=av+bv.

The elements of VVV are called vectors, whatever they actually are.

First consequences

Proposition. In any vector space: (a) the zero vector is unique; (b) each v\mathbf{v}v has exactly one additive inverse, written −v-\mathbf{v}−v; (c) 0v=00\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}0v=0; (d) a0=0a\mathbf{0} = \mathbf{0}a0=0; (e) (−1)v=−v(-1)\mathbf{v} = -\mathbf{v}(−1)v=−v.

Proof. (a) If 0\mathbf{0}0 and 0′\mathbf{0}'0′ are both identities, 0=0+0′=0′\mathbf{0} = \mathbf{0} + \mathbf{0}' = \mathbf{0}'0=0+0′=0′. (b) If w,w′\mathbf{w}, \mathbf{w}'w,w′ are both inverses of v\mathbf{v}v, then w=w+(v+w′)=(w+v)+w′=w′\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{w} + (\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{w}') = (\mathbf{w} + \mathbf{v}) + \mathbf{w}' = \mathbf{w}'w=w+(v+w′)=(w+v)+w′=w′. (c) 0v=(0+0)v=0v+0v0\mathbf{v} = (0 + 0)\mathbf{v} = 0\mathbf{v} + 0\mathbf{v}0v=(0+0)v=0v+0v; add −(0v)-(0\mathbf{v})−(0v) to both sides. (d) The same with a0=a(0+0)a\mathbf{0} = a(\mathbf{0} + \mathbf{0})a0=a(0+0). (e) v+(−1)v=(1+(−1))v=0v=0\mathbf{v} + (-1)\mathbf{v} = (1 + (-1))\mathbf{v} = 0\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}v+(−1)v=(1+(−1))v=0v=0, so (−1)v(-1)\mathbf{v}(−1)v is the inverse of v\mathbf{v}v, by (b). ■\blacksquare■

Chapter 2 — Subspaces

Terminology

  • Subspace — a subset U⊆VU \subseteq VU⊆V that is itself a vector space with the same addition and scalar multiplication.

Theorem (subspace test). A subset UUU of a vector space VVV is a subspace if and only if

  1. 0∈U\mathbf{0} \in U0∈U;
  2. u,w∈U⇒u+w∈U\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{w} \in U \Rightarrow \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{w} \in Uu,w∈U⇒u+w∈U (closed under addition);
  3. a∈Fa \in Fa∈F, u∈U⇒au∈U\mathbf{u} \in U \Rightarrow a\mathbf{u} \in Uu∈U⇒au∈U (closed under scalar multiplication).

Proof. A subspace clearly satisfies 2 and 3, and it contains its own zero vector z\mathbf{z}z with z+z=z\mathbf{z} + \mathbf{z} = \mathbf{z}z+z=z; adding −z-\mathbf{z}−z in VVV shows z=0\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{0}z=0, so 1 holds. Conversely, suppose 1–3 hold. Conditions 2 and 3 make addition and scalar multiplication land in UUU. Axioms 1, 2, 5–8 are identities that hold for all vectors of VVV, so in particular for those of UUU. Axiom 3 holds by condition 1. For axiom 4: if u∈U\mathbf{u} \in Uu∈U then −u=(−1)u∈U-\mathbf{u} = (-1)\mathbf{u} \in U−u=(−1)u∈U by condition 3 and part (e) of the proposition. ■\blacksquare■

Trick: conditions 2 and 3 together are the same as "closed under linear combinations": au+bw∈Ua\mathbf{u} + b\mathbf{w} \in Uau+bw∈U for all u,w∈U\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{w} \in Uu,w∈U and scalars a,ba, ba,b. Check 0\mathbf{0}0 first — it is the fastest way to reject a non-subspace.

Examples and non-examples

  • Null space N(A)={x∈Fn:Ax=0}N(A) = \{\mathbf{x} \in F^n : A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}\}N(A)={x∈Fn:Ax=0} is a subspace of FnF^nFn: A0=0A\mathbf{0} = \mathbf{0}A0=0, and A(au+bw)=aAu+bAw=0A(a\mathbf{u} + b\mathbf{w}) = aA\mathbf{u} + bA\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{0}A(au+bw)=aAu+bAw=0.
  • Column space C(A)={Ax:x∈Fn}C(A) = \{A\mathbf{x} : \mathbf{x} \in F^n\}C(A)={Ax:x∈Fn}, the span of the columns, is a subspace of FmF^mFm.
  • {p∈P2(R):p(1)=0}\{p \in \mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb{R}) : p(1) = 0\}{p∈P2​(R):p(1)=0} is a subspace; {p:p(1)=5}\{p : p(1) = 5\}{p:p(1)=5} is not (no zero polynomial).
  • The symmetric n×nn \times nn×n matrices form a subspace of Mn×nM_{n \times n}Mn×n​.
  • The solutions yyy of y′′+y=0y'' + y = 0y′′+y=0 form a subspace of the twice-differentiable functions R→R\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}R→R.
  • The solutions of Ax=bA\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}Ax=b with b≠0\mathbf{b} \neq \mathbf{0}b=0 are not a subspace (Linear Algebra 00, Chapter 7): 0\mathbf{0}0 is not a solution.
  • The union of the xxx-axis and the yyy-axis in R2\mathbb{R}^2R2 is not a subspace: (1,0)+(0,1)=(1,1)(1, 0) + (0, 1) = (1, 1)(1,0)+(0,1)=(1,1) is in neither.

Intersections are subspaces. If UUU and WWW are subspaces, so is U∩WU \cap WU∩W: it contains 0\mathbf{0}0, and a linear combination of vectors in both lies in both. Unions usually are not, as the axes show; Chapter 8 replaces the union by the sum U+WU + WU+W.

Chapter 3 — Span and linear independence in general

The definitions from Linear Algebra 00 carry over unchanged. For a finite list v1,…,vk\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_kv1​,…,vk​ in VVV:

  • span⁡(v1,…,vk)\operatorname{span}(\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_k)span(v1​,…,vk​) is the set of all linear combinations a1v1+⋯+akvka_1\mathbf{v}_1 + \dots + a_k\mathbf{v}_ka1​v1​+⋯+ak​vk​. By convention the span of the empty list is {0}\{\mathbf{0}\}{0}.
  • The list spans VVV if its span is all of VVV.
  • The list is linearly independent if a1v1+⋯+akvk=0a_1\mathbf{v}_1 + \dots + a_k\mathbf{v}_k = \mathbf{0}a1​v1​+⋯+ak​vk​=0 forces a1=⋯=ak=0a_1 = \dots = a_k = 0a1​=⋯=ak​=0; otherwise it is dependent. The empty list is independent.

Proposition. span⁡(v1,…,vk)\operatorname{span}(\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_k)span(v1​,…,vk​) is the smallest subspace of VVV containing every vi\mathbf{v}_ivi​.

Proof. It contains 0\mathbf{0}0, and a combination of combinations is a combination, so it is a subspace; it contains each vi\mathbf{v}_ivi​. Any subspace containing all vi\mathbf{v}_ivi​ is closed under linear combinations, so it contains the span. ■\blacksquare■

The linear dependence lemma

Lemma. If v1,…,vm\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_mv1​,…,vm​ is linearly dependent, then there is an index jjj such that

  1. vj∈span⁡(v1,…,vj−1)\mathbf{v}_j \in \operatorname{span}(\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_{j-1})vj​∈span(v1​,…,vj−1​), and
  2. removing vj\mathbf{v}_jvj​ from the list does not change its span.

Proof. Take a relation a1v1+⋯+amvm=0a_1\mathbf{v}_1 + \dots + a_m\mathbf{v}_m = \mathbf{0}a1​v1​+⋯+am​vm​=0 with not all ai=0a_i = 0ai​=0, and let jjj be the largest index with aj≠0a_j \neq 0aj​=0. Then

vj=−a1ajv1−⋯−aj−1ajvj−1,\mathbf{v}_j = -\frac{a_1}{a_j}\mathbf{v}_1 - \dots - \frac{a_{j-1}}{a_j}\mathbf{v}_{j-1}, vj​=−aj​a1​​v1​−⋯−aj​aj−1​​vj−1​,

which proves 1. (If j=1j = 1j=1 this says v1=0\mathbf{v}_1 = \mathbf{0}v1​=0, the span of the empty list.) For 2, in any combination of the full list, replace vj\mathbf{v}_jvj​ by the right-hand side above; the result is a combination of the list without vj\mathbf{v}_jvj​. ■\blacksquare■

Independence outside Fⁿ

  • In P2(R)\mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb{R})P2​(R), the list 1,t,t21, t, t^21,t,t2 is independent: if a+bt+ct2a + bt + ct^2a+bt+ct2 is the zero polynomial, all its coefficients are 0.
  • In the functions R→R\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}R→R, sin⁡\sinsin and cos⁡\coscos are independent: if asin⁡x+bcos⁡x=0a\sin x + b\cos x = 0asinx+bcosx=0 for all xxx, then x=0x = 0x=0 gives b=0b = 0b=0 and x=π/2x = \pi/2x=π/2 gives a=0a = 0a=0.

Common pitfall: "asin⁡x+bcos⁡x=0a\sin x + b\cos x = 0asinx+bcosx=0" means equality as functions, for every xxx. Finding one xxx where a combination is zero proves nothing; you must show the combination is zero everywhere only when all weights are zero.

Chapter 4 — Basis, the exchange lemma and dimension

Terminology

  • Basis of VVV — a list of vectors in VVV that is linearly independent and spans VVV.
  • Finite-dimensional — VVV is spanned by some finite list. Otherwise infinite-dimensional.
  • Standard basis of FnF^nFn — e1,…,en\mathbf{e}_1, \dots, \mathbf{e}_ne1​,…,en​. Of Pn(F)\mathcal{P}_n(F)Pn​(F) — 1,t,…,tn1, t, \dots, t^n1,t,…,tn.

Theorem (unique representation). A list v1,…,vn\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_nv1​,…,vn​ is a basis of VVV if and only if every v∈V\mathbf{v} \in Vv∈V can be written as a1v1+⋯+anvna_1\mathbf{v}_1 + \dots + a_n\mathbf{v}_na1​v1​+⋯+an​vn​ in exactly one way.

Proof. Spanning is "at least one way". If a basis gave two ways, subtracting them gives ∑(ai−bi)vi=0\sum (a_i - b_i)\mathbf{v}_i = \mathbf{0}∑(ai​−bi​)vi​=0, so every ai=bia_i = b_iai​=bi​ by independence. Conversely, uniqueness for v=0\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}v=0 (which is 0v1+⋯+0vn0\mathbf{v}_1 + \dots + 0\mathbf{v}_n0v1​+⋯+0vn​) is exactly independence. ■\blacksquare■

The Steinitz exchange lemma

Lemma (Steinitz exchange). Let VVV be a vector space. Suppose u1,…,um\mathbf{u}_1, \dots, \mathbf{u}_mu1​,…,um​ is linearly independent in VVV and w1,…,wn\mathbf{w}_1, \dots, \mathbf{w}_nw1​,…,wn​ spans VVV. Then m≤nm \le nm≤n. Moreover, after renumbering the w\mathbf{w}w's, the list

u1,…,um,wm+1,…,wn\mathbf{u}_1, \dots, \mathbf{u}_m, \mathbf{w}_{m+1}, \dots, \mathbf{w}_n u1​,…,um​,wm+1​,…,wn​

also spans VVV.

Proof. We show by induction on k=0,1,…,mk = 0, 1, \dots, mk=0,1,…,m that k≤nk \le nk≤n and that, after renumbering, u1,…,uk,wk+1,…,wn\mathbf{u}_1, \dots, \mathbf{u}_k, \mathbf{w}_{k+1}, \dots, \mathbf{w}_nu1​,…,uk​,wk+1​,…,wn​ spans VVV. For k=0k = 0k=0 this is the hypothesis.

Assume it holds for some k<mk < mk<m. Since the list u1,…,uk,wk+1,…,wn\mathbf{u}_1, \dots, \mathbf{u}_k, \mathbf{w}_{k+1}, \dots, \mathbf{w}_nu1​,…,uk​,wk+1​,…,wn​ spans VVV, we can write

uk+1=a1u1+⋯+akuk+bk+1wk+1+⋯+bnwn.\mathbf{u}_{k+1} = a_1\mathbf{u}_1 + \dots + a_k\mathbf{u}_k + b_{k+1}\mathbf{w}_{k+1} + \dots + b_n\mathbf{w}_n. uk+1​=a1​u1​+⋯+ak​uk​+bk+1​wk+1​+⋯+bn​wn​.

If every bjb_jbj​ were 0 (in particular, if no w\mathbf{w}w's were left, k=nk = nk=n), then uk+1\mathbf{u}_{k+1}uk+1​ would be a combination of u1,…,uk\mathbf{u}_1, \dots, \mathbf{u}_ku1​,…,uk​, contradicting independence of the u\mathbf{u}u's. So some bj≠0b_j \neq 0bj​=0; hence k+1≤nk + 1 \le nk+1≤n. Renumber so that bk+1≠0b_{k+1} \neq 0bk+1​=0 and solve for wk+1\mathbf{w}_{k+1}wk+1​:

wk+1=1bk+1(uk+1−∑i=1kaiui−∑j=k+2nbjwj).\mathbf{w}_{k+1} = \frac{1}{b_{k+1}}\Bigl(\mathbf{u}_{k+1} - \sum_{i=1}^{k} a_i\mathbf{u}_i - \sum_{j=k+2}^{n} b_j\mathbf{w}_j\Bigr). wk+1​=bk+1​1​(uk+1​−i=1∑k​ai​ui​−j=k+2∑n​bj​wj​).

So wk+1\mathbf{w}_{k+1}wk+1​ lies in the span of u1,…,uk+1,wk+2,…,wn\mathbf{u}_1, \dots, \mathbf{u}_{k+1}, \mathbf{w}_{k+2}, \dots, \mathbf{w}_nu1​,…,uk+1​,wk+2​,…,wn​. That span therefore contains the whole old spanning list, so it is VVV. This completes the step. At k=mk = mk=m we get m≤nm \le nm≤n and the stated spanning list. ■\blacksquare■

Small example. In R3\mathbb{R}^3R3 take the independent u1=(1,1,0)\mathbf{u}_1 = (1, 1, 0)u1​=(1,1,0), u2=(0,1,1)\mathbf{u}_2 = (0, 1, 1)u2​=(0,1,1) and the spanning e1,e2,e3\mathbf{e}_1, \mathbf{e}_2, \mathbf{e}_3e1​,e2​,e3​. Since u1=e1+e2\mathbf{u}_1 = \mathbf{e}_1 + \mathbf{e}_2u1​=e1​+e2​ has a nonzero coefficient on e1\mathbf{e}_1e1​, swap it out: u1,e2,e3\mathbf{u}_1, \mathbf{e}_2, \mathbf{e}_3u1​,e2​,e3​ spans. Then u2=0 u1+e2+e3\mathbf{u}_2 = 0\,\mathbf{u}_1 + \mathbf{e}_2 + \mathbf{e}_3u2​=0u1​+e2​+e3​; swap out e2\mathbf{e}_2e2​: u1,u2,e3\mathbf{u}_1, \mathbf{u}_2, \mathbf{e}_3u1​,u2​,e3​ spans R3\mathbb{R}^3R3. (Three vectors that span R3\mathbb{R}^3R3 are automatically a basis — see the theorem at the end of this chapter.)

Dimension is well defined

Theorem. In a finite-dimensional vector space, any two bases have the same length.

Proof. Let B1B_1B1​ and B2B_2B2​ be bases, of lengths mmm and nnn. B1B_1B1​ is independent and B2B_2B2​ spans, so m≤nm \le nm≤n by Steinitz. Swap roles: n≤mn \le mn≤m. ■\blacksquare■

This common length is the dimension dim⁡V\dim VdimV.

Watch out: Cn\mathbb{C}^nCn has dimension nnn over C\mathbb{C}C but 2n2n2n over R\mathbb{R}R (a basis over R\mathbb{R}R is e1,ie1,…,en,ien\mathbf{e}_1, i\mathbf{e}_1, \dots, \mathbf{e}_n, i\mathbf{e}_ne1​,ie1​,…,en​,ien​). Dimension depends on the field of scalars.

Growing and shrinking to a basis

Theorem. Let VVV be finite-dimensional with dim⁡V=n\dim V = ndimV=n.

  1. Every spanning list can be shrunk to a basis by removing vectors.
  2. Every independent list can be extended to a basis by adding vectors.
  3. Any nnn independent vectors form a basis; any nnn spanning vectors form a basis.
  4. Every subspace UUU is finite-dimensional with dim⁡U≤n\dim U \le ndimU≤n, and dim⁡U=n\dim U = ndimU=n only if U=VU = VU=V.

Proof. (1) While the list is dependent, the dependence lemma lets you remove one vector without changing the span. The process stops at an independent spanning list. (2) Apply Steinitz with a basis as the spanning list: the independent list plus the remaining n−mn - mn−m basis vectors spans VVV; it has length nnn, and by (1) some sublist is a basis, which must have length nnn, so it is the whole list. (3) An independent list of length nnn extends to a basis of length nnn, so nothing is added; a spanning list of length nnn shrinks to a basis of length nnn, so nothing is removed. (4) Any independent list in UUU is independent in VVV, so it has length at most nnn by Steinitz. Keep adding vectors of UUU not yet in the span of an independent list (independence is kept, by Exercise 7); this stops after at most nnn steps with a basis of UUU. If dim⁡U=n\dim U = ndimU=n, that basis is nnn independent vectors of VVV, so by (3) it spans VVV, hence U=VU = VU=V. ■\blacksquare■

Chapter 5 — Coordinates

If B=(v1,…,vn)B = (\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_n)B=(v1​,…,vn​) is a basis of VVV, each v\mathbf{v}v has unique weights with v=a1v1+⋯+anvn\mathbf{v} = a_1\mathbf{v}_1 + \dots + a_n\mathbf{v}_nv=a1​v1​+⋯+an​vn​. The column [v]B=(a1,…,an)∈Fn[\mathbf{v}]_B = (a_1, \dots, a_n) \in F^n[v]B​=(a1​,…,an​)∈Fn is the coordinate vector of v\mathbf{v}v relative to BBB.

The map v↦[v]B\mathbf{v} \mapsto [\mathbf{v}]_Bv↦[v]B​ is one-to-one, onto FnF^nFn, and respects linear combinations: [au+bw]B=a[u]B+b[w]B[a\mathbf{u} + b\mathbf{w}]_B = a[\mathbf{u}]_B + b[\mathbf{w}]_B[au+bw]B​=a[u]B​+b[w]B​. So every nnn-dimensional space over FFF behaves exactly like FnF^nFn, and computations in it can be done with columns and matrices. Linear Algebra 03 makes this precise (isomorphism) and studies how coordinates change when the basis changes.

Example in R2\mathbb{R}^2R2. With B=((1,1),(1,−1))B = ((1, 1), (1, -1))B=((1,1),(1,−1)) and x=(3,1)\mathbf{x} = (3, 1)x=(3,1): solve a(1,1)+b(1,−1)=(3,1)a(1,1) + b(1,-1) = (3, 1)a(1,1)+b(1,−1)=(3,1), so a+b=3a + b = 3a+b=3, a−b=1a - b = 1a−b=1, giving a=2a = 2a=2, b=1b = 1b=1. So [x]B=(2,1)[\mathbf{x}]_B = (2, 1)[x]B​=(2,1), while the standard coordinates are (3,1)(3, 1)(3,1) — same vector, different description.

(the weights on 111, 1+t1 + t1+t and (1+t)2(1 + t)^2(1+t)2, in that order). Check: (1+2t+t2)−2−2t+1=t2(1 + 2t + t^2) - 2 - 2t + 1 = t^2(1+2t+t2)−2−2t+1=t2.

Chapter 6 — The four fundamental subspaces

Terminology

For an m×nm \times nm×n matrix AAA of rank rrr (the number of pivots):

Subspace Symbol Lives in Definition
Column space C(A)C(A)C(A) FmF^mFm all AxA\mathbf{x}Ax; span of the columns
Null space N(A)N(A)N(A) FnF^nFn all x\mathbf{x}x with Ax=0A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}Ax=0
Row space C(AT)C(A^T)C(AT) FnF^nFn span of the rows
Left null space N(AT)N(A^T)N(AT) FmF^mFm all y\mathbf{y}y with ATy=0A^T\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{0}ATy=0, that is yTA=0T\mathbf{y}^TA = \mathbf{0}^TyTA=0T

Two facts about row operations

Let EA=REA = REA=R with EEE invertible (a product of elementary matrices) and RRR the RREF.

Fact 1 — the row space does not change. Every row of RRR is a combination of rows of AAA, and since A=E−1RA = E^{-1}RA=E−1R, every row of AAA is a combination of rows of RRR. So C(AT)=C(RT)C(A^T) = C(R^T)C(AT)=C(RT).

Fact 2 — linear relations among columns do not change. Ax=0  ⟺  EAx=0  ⟺  Rx=0A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0} \iff EA\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0} \iff R\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}Ax=0⟺EAx=0⟺Rx=0, because EEE is invertible. So a combination of columns of AAA is zero exactly when the same combination of columns of RRR is zero, and N(A)=N(R)N(A) = N(R)N(A)=N(R). (The column spaces of AAA and RRR usually differ.)

Bases from the RREF

  • C(A)C(A)C(A) — the pivot columns of AAA (not of RRR). In RRR the pivot columns are distinct standard basis vectors, so they are independent, and every other column is a combination of them. By Fact 2 the same holds for the corresponding columns of AAA.
  • C(AT)C(A^T)C(AT) — the nonzero rows of RRR. They span the row space by Fact 1, and they are independent because each has a leading 1 in a column where the other rows have 0.
  • N(A)N(A)N(A) — the n−rn - rn−r special solutions (one free variable 1, the others 0), as in Linear Algebra 00.
  • N(AT)N(A^T)N(AT) — the last m−rm - rm−r rows of EEE: those rows multiply AAA to give the zero rows of RRR.

Worked example

A=(1222246836810),R=(120−200120000),m=3, n=4, r=2.A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 & 6 & 8 \\ 3 & 6 & 8 & 10 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad R = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad m = 3,\ n = 4,\ r = 2. The other columns satisfy the same relations as in RRR: column 2 =2×= 2 \times=2× column 1, and column 4 =−2×= -2 \times=−2× column 1 +2×+ 2 \times+2× column 3. Orthogonality — a preview

Each row of AAA dotted with a null-space vector gives 0 — that is what Ax=0A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}Ax=0 says, one row at a time. So every vector of N(A)N(A)N(A) is orthogonal to every vector of C(AT)C(A^T)C(AT). In the example, (1,2,0,−2)⋅(−2,1,0,0)=0(1, 2, 0, -2)\cdot(-2, 1, 0, 0) = 0(1,2,0,−2)⋅(−2,1,0,0)=0, (1,2,0,−2)⋅(2,0,−2,1)=0(1, 2, 0, -2)\cdot(2, 0, -2, 1) = 0(1,2,0,−2)⋅(2,0,−2,1)=0, (0,0,1,2)⋅(−2,1,0,0)=0(0, 0, 1, 2)\cdot(-2, 1, 0, 0) = 0(0,0,1,2)⋅(−2,1,0,0)=0 and (0,0,1,2)⋅(2,0,−2,1)=0(0, 0, 1, 2)\cdot(2, 0, -2, 1) = 0(0,0,1,2)⋅(2,0,−2,1)=0. In the same way N(AT)N(A^T)N(AT) is orthogonal to C(A)C(A)C(A): (−1,−1,1)⋅(1,2,3)=0(-1, -1, 1)\cdot(1, 2, 3) = 0(−1,−1,1)⋅(1,2,3)=0 and (−1,−1,1)⋅(2,6,8)=0(-1, -1, 1)\cdot(2, 6, 8) = 0(−1,−1,1)⋅(2,6,8)=0. Over R\mathbb{R}R the dimensions add up (2+2=42 + 2 = 42+2=4, 2+1=32 + 1 = 32+1=3), which makes each pair orthogonal complements — proved in Linear Algebra 05.

Row rank equals column rank

Theorem. For every matrix, dim⁡C(A)=dim⁡C(AT)=r\dim C(A) = \dim C(A^T) = rdimC(A)=dimC(AT)=r, the number of pivots.

Proof. The pivot columns of AAA are a basis of C(A)C(A)C(A), and there are rrr of them. The nonzero rows of RRR are a basis of C(AT)C(A^T)C(AT), and there are rrr of them (one per pivot). ■\blacksquare■

This is not obvious: for a 3×1003 \times 1003×100 matrix it says that the 100 columns span a space of the same dimension as the 3 rows. It also shows rank⁡A=rank⁡AT\operatorname{rank} A = \operatorname{rank} A^TrankA=rankAT, and that r≤min⁡(m,n)r \le \min(m, n)r≤min(m,n).

Rank-one matrices. A matrix has rank 1 exactly when it is a nonzero column times a nonzero row, A=uvTA = \mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}^TA=uvT: every column is a multiple of u\mathbf{u}u, every row a multiple of vT\mathbf{v}^TvT. The outer-product view of Linear Algebra 01 writes any ABABAB as a sum of such pieces.

Chapter 7 — Rank–nullity (matrix form)

Theorem (rank–nullity). For an m×nm \times nm×n matrix AAA,

dim⁡C(A)+dim⁡N(A)=n.\dim C(A) + \dim N(A) = n. dimC(A)+dimN(A)=n.

Proof. Let rrr be the number of pivots. dim⁡C(A)=r\dim C(A) = rdimC(A)=r by Chapter 6. It remains to show that the n−rn - rn−r special solutions s1,…,sn−r\mathbf{s}_1, \dots, \mathbf{s}_{n-r}s1​,…,sn−r​ are a basis of N(A)N(A)N(A).

Independent: look only at the free-variable entries. In sk\mathbf{s}_ksk​ the kkk-th free variable is 1 and the others are 0. So in ∑cksk\sum c_k\mathbf{s}_k∑ck​sk​ the kkk-th free entry is ckc_kck​; if the sum is 0\mathbf{0}0, every ck=0c_k = 0ck​=0.

Spanning: let x∈N(A)\mathbf{x} \in N(A)x∈N(A) with free-variable values f1,…,fn−rf_1, \dots, f_{n-r}f1​,…,fn−r​. Then z=x−∑fksk\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{x} - \sum f_k\mathbf{s}_kz=x−∑fk​sk​ is in N(A)N(A)N(A) and has every free variable equal to 0. The RREF expresses each basic variable in terms of the free ones, so all basic variables of z\mathbf{z}z are 0 too; thus z=0\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{0}z=0 and x=∑fksk\mathbf{x} = \sum f_k\mathbf{s}_kx=∑fk​sk​.

So dim⁡N(A)=n−r\dim N(A) = n - rdimN(A)=n−r, and r+(n−r)=nr + (n - r) = nr+(n−r)=n. ■\blacksquare■

In words: each of the nnn columns either contributes a pivot (a new direction in the column space) or a free variable (a new direction in the null space). For the example, 2+2=42 + 2 = 42+2=4. Applied to ATA^TAT (which has mmm columns and the same rank), it gives dim⁡N(AT)=m−r\dim N(A^T) = m - rdimN(AT)=m−r, here 3−2=13 - 2 = 13−2=1.

The general version — for a linear map T:V→WT : V \to WT:V→W, dim⁡V=dim⁡im⁡T+dim⁡ker⁡T\dim V = \dim \operatorname{im} T + \dim \ker TdimV=dimimT+dimkerT — is proved in Linear Algebra 03.

Chapter 8 — Sums and direct sums

Terminology

  • Sum of subspaces U,W⊆VU, W \subseteq VU,W⊆V: U+W={u+w:u∈U,w∈W}U + W = \{\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{w} : \mathbf{u} \in U, \mathbf{w} \in W\}U+W={u+w:u∈U,w∈W}. It is the smallest subspace containing both (a subspace containing UUU and WWW contains all such sums).
  • Direct sum — the sum is direct, written U⊕WU \oplus WU⊕W, if every vector of U+WU + WU+W can be written as u+w\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{w}u+w in only one way.

Proposition. U+WU + WU+W is direct if and only if U∩W={0}U \cap W = \{\mathbf{0}\}U∩W={0}.

Proof. Suppose the sum is direct and v∈U∩W\mathbf{v} \in U \cap Wv∈U∩W. Then 0=v+(−v)\mathbf{0} = \mathbf{v} + (-\mathbf{v})0=v+(−v) with v∈U\mathbf{v} \in Uv∈U, −v∈W-\mathbf{v} \in W−v∈W, and also 0=0+0\mathbf{0} = \mathbf{0} + \mathbf{0}0=0+0; uniqueness gives v=0\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}v=0. Conversely, if U∩W={0}U \cap W = \{\mathbf{0}\}U∩W={0} and u+w=u′+w′\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{w} = \mathbf{u}' + \mathbf{w}'u+w=u′+w′, then u−u′=w′−w\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{u}' = \mathbf{w}' - \mathbf{w}u−u′=w′−w lies in both UUU and WWW, so it is 0\mathbf{0}0. ■\blacksquare■

Watch out: for three or more subspaces, pairwise zero intersections are not enough. Three distinct lines through the origin in R2\mathbb{R}^2R2 meet pairwise only at 0\mathbf{0}0, but their sum is not direct (three vectors in R2\mathbb{R}^2R2 are dependent).

The dimension formula

Theorem. If UUU and WWW are finite-dimensional subspaces of VVV, then

dim⁡(U+W)=dim⁡U+dim⁡W−dim⁡(U∩W).\dim(U + W) = \dim U + \dim W - \dim(U \cap W). dim(U+W)=dimU+dimW−dim(U∩W).

Proof. Let z1,…,zk\mathbf{z}_1, \dots, \mathbf{z}_kz1​,…,zk​ be a basis of U∩WU \cap WU∩W. Extend it to a basis z1,…,zk,u1,…,up\mathbf{z}_1, \dots, \mathbf{z}_k, \mathbf{u}_1, \dots, \mathbf{u}_pz1​,…,zk​,u1​,…,up​ of UUU and to a basis z1,…,zk,w1,…,wq\mathbf{z}_1, \dots, \mathbf{z}_k, \mathbf{w}_1, \dots, \mathbf{w}_qz1​,…,zk​,w1​,…,wq​ of WWW (Chapter 4). For independence, suppose

Now ∑aizi+∑bjuj=0\sum a_i\mathbf{z}_i + \sum b_j\mathbf{u}_j = \mathbf{0}∑ai​zi​+∑bj​uj​=0 is a relation in a basis of UUU, so all ai,bj=0a_i, b_j = 0ai​,bj​=0. Hence the combined list is a basis, and

dim⁡(U+W)=k+p+q=(k+p)+(k+q)−k.■\dim(U + W) = k + p + q = (k + p) + (k + q) - k. \qquad \blacksquare dim(U+W)=k+p+q=(k+p)+(k+q)−k.■

This is the same shape as ∣A∪B∣=∣A∣+∣B∣−∣A∩B∣\lvert A \cup B\rvert = \lvert A\rvert + \lvert B\rvert - \lvert A \cap B\rvert∣A∪B∣=∣A∣+∣B∣−∣A∩B∣ for finite sets.

Practice Exercises

Exercise 1 — A polynomial subspace

Show that U={p∈P2(R):p(1)=0}U = \{p \in \mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb{R}) : p(1) = 0\}U={p∈P2​(R):p(1)=0} is a subspace, and find a basis and its dimension.

Solution

The zero polynomial has p(1)=0p(1) = 0p(1)=0, and (ap+bq)(1)=ap(1)+bq(1)=0(ap + bq)(1) = ap(1) + bq(1) = 0(ap+bq)(1)=ap(1)+bq(1)=0, so UUU is a subspace. p(t)=c0+c1t+c2t2p(t) = c_0 + c_1t + c_2t^2p(t)=c0​+c1​t+c2​t2 is in UUU iff c0+c1+c2=0c_0 + c_1 + c_2 = 0c0​+c1​+c2​=0, i.e. c0=−c1−c2c_0 = -c_1 - c_2c0​=−c1​−c2​, so p=c1(t−1)+c2(t2−1)p = c_1(t - 1) + c_2(t^2 - 1)p=c1​(t−1)+c2​(t2−1). The list t−1t - 1t−1, t2−1t^2 - 1t2−1 spans UUU and is independent (only the second has a t2t^2t2 term), so dim⁡U=2\dim U = 2dimU=2. This matches rank–nullity: UUU is the null space of the map p↦p(1)p \mapsto p(1)p↦p(1), and 3−1=23 - 1 = 23−1=2.

Exercise 2 — Not a subspace

Is {(x,y)∈R2:xy≥0}\{(x, y) \in \mathbb{R}^2 : xy \ge 0\}{(x,y)∈R2:xy≥0} a subspace?

Solution

No. It contains 0\mathbf{0}0 and is closed under scalar multiplication ((cx)(cy)=c2xy≥0(cx)(cy) = c^2xy \ge 0(cx)(cy)=c2xy≥0), but not under addition: (1,0)+(0,−1)=(1,−1)(1, 0) + (0, -1) = (1, -1)(1,0)+(0,−1)=(1,−1) has xy=−1<0xy = -1 < 0xy=−1<0. It is the union of the first and third quadrants.

Exercise 3 — Shrink to a basis

Find a basis for span⁡{(1,2,1),(2,4,2),(1,0,1),(0,1,0)}\operatorname{span}\{(1, 2, 1), (2, 4, 2), (1, 0, 1), (0, 1, 0)\}span{(1,2,1),(2,4,2),(1,0,1),(0,1,0)} taken from the given vectors, and its dimension.

Solution

Put them as columns and row reduce: (121024011210)→(1201/2001−1/20000)\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 4 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \to \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 & 1/2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -1/2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}​121​242​101​010​​→​100​200​010​1/2−1/20​​. Pivot columns 1 and 3, so (1,2,1)(1, 2, 1)(1,2,1) and (1,0,1)(1, 0, 1)(1,0,1) are a basis and the dimension is 2. (All four vectors satisfy x1=x3x_1 = x_3x1​=x3​, a plane.)

Exercise 4 — Four subspaces of a rank-one matrix

For B=(122436)B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \\ 3 & 6 \end{pmatrix}B=​123​246​​, give bases and dimensions of all four subspaces.

Solution

m=3m = 3m=3, n=2n = 2n=2, r=1r = 1r=1 (B=(1,2,3)T(1,2)B = (1, 2, 3)^T(1, 2)B=(1,2,3)T(1,2)). C(B)C(B)C(B): (1,2,3)(1, 2, 3)(1,2,3), dimension 1. C(BT)C(B^T)C(BT): (1,2)(1, 2)(1,2), dimension 1. N(B)N(B)N(B): (−2,1)(-2, 1)(−2,1), dimension n−r=1n - r = 1n−r=1. N(BT)N(B^T)N(BT): solutions of y1+2y2+3y3=0y_1 + 2y_2 + 3y_3 = 0y1​+2y2​+3y3​=0, basis (−2,1,0)(-2, 1, 0)(−2,1,0), (−3,0,1)(-3, 0, 1)(−3,0,1), dimension m−r=2m - r = 2m−r=2. Check orthogonality: (1,2)⋅(−2,1)=0(1, 2)\cdot(-2, 1) = 0(1,2)⋅(−2,1)=0.

Exercise 5 — Coordinates

Find the coordinates of p(t)=2+3t+t2p(t) = 2 + 3t + t^2p(t)=2+3t+t2 relative to B=(1, 1+t, (1+t)2)B = (1,\ 1 + t,\ (1 + t)^2)B=(1, 1+t, (1+t)2).

Solution

(1+t)2=1+2t+t2(1 + t)^2 = 1 + 2t + t^2(1+t)2=1+2t+t2, so p−(1+t)2=1+tp - (1 + t)^2 = 1 + tp−(1+t)2=1+t. Hence p=0⋅1+1⋅(1+t)+1⋅(1+t)2p = 0 \cdot 1 + 1 \cdot (1 + t) + 1 \cdot (1 + t)^2p=0⋅1+1⋅(1+t)+1⋅(1+t)2, and [p]B=(0,1,1)[p]_B = (0, 1, 1)[p]B​=(0,1,1). Check: (1+t)+(1+2t+t2)=2+3t+t2(1 + t) + (1 + 2t + t^2) = 2 + 3t + t^2(1+t)+(1+2t+t2)=2+3t+t2.

Exercise 6 — Forced intersection

Let UUU and WWW be 3-dimensional subspaces of R5\mathbb{R}^5R5. Prove that U∩W≠{0}U \cap W \neq \{\mathbf{0}\}U∩W={0}.

Solution

U+W⊆R5U + W \subseteq \mathbb{R}^5U+W⊆R5, so dim⁡(U+W)≤5\dim(U + W) \le 5dim(U+W)≤5. The dimension formula gives dim⁡(U∩W)=3+3−dim⁡(U+W)≥6−5=1\dim(U \cap W) = 3 + 3 - \dim(U + W) \ge 6 - 5 = 1dim(U∩W)=3+3−dim(U+W)≥6−5=1.

Exercise 7 — Proof practice

Prove that if v1,…,vm\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_mv1​,…,vm​ is independent and v∉span⁡(v1,…,vm)\mathbf{v} \notin \operatorname{span}(\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_m)v∈/span(v1​,…,vm​), then v1,…,vm,v\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_m, \mathbf{v}v1​,…,vm​,v is independent.

Solution

Suppose a1v1+⋯+amvm+av=0a_1\mathbf{v}_1 + \dots + a_m\mathbf{v}_m + a\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}a1​v1​+⋯+am​vm​+av=0. If a≠0a \neq 0a=0, then v=−1a∑aivi\mathbf{v} = -\frac1a\sum a_i\mathbf{v}_iv=−a1​∑ai​vi​ is in the span — a contradiction. So a=0a = 0a=0, and then all ai=0a_i = 0ai​=0 by independence of the vi\mathbf{v}_ivi​. (This is the step used in Chapter 4, part 4.)

What's next

Linear Algebra 03 moves from spaces to maps between them. A linear map T:V→WT : V \to WT:V→W is determined by what it does to a basis, so after choosing bases it becomes a matrix — and changing the bases changes the matrix to Q−1APQ^{-1}APQ−1AP (or P−1APP^{-1}APP−1AP for an operator). The post proves the full rank–nullity theorem for linear maps, defines isomorphism (why every nnn-dimensional space "is" FnF^nFn), and then builds the determinant from its defining properties, with its geometric meaning as a signed volume scale factor.

References

  • Sheldon Axler, Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th edition, Springer (Undergraduate Texts in Mathematics), 2024 — Chapters 1–2 (vector spaces, subspaces, sums and direct sums, span, independence, bases, dimension, the linear dependence lemma). Open access at linear.axler.net.
  • Kenneth Hoffman and Ray Kunze, Linear Algebra, 2nd edition, Prentice-Hall, 1971 — Chapter 2 (vector spaces, bases and dimension, coordinates, row-equivalence).
  • Gilbert Strang, Introduction to Linear Algebra, 6th edition, Wellesley-Cambridge Press, 2023 — Chapter 3 (the four fundamental subspaces, rank, dimensions).
  • Gilbert Strang, "The Fundamental Theorem of Linear Algebra", The American Mathematical Monthly 100(9), 1993, pp. 848–855 — the source of the four-subspace picture.
  • David C. Lay, Steven R. Lay and Judi J. McDonald, Linear Algebra and Its Applications, 6th edition, Pearson, 2021 — Chapter 4 (vector spaces, null and column spaces, bases, coordinate systems, dimension, rank).
  • MIT OpenCourseWare, 18.06 Linear Algebra, Spring 2010 (Gilbert Strang) — Lectures 5–10: vector spaces, column and null spaces, solving Ax=0A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}Ax=0 and Ax=bA\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}Ax=b, independence, basis and dimension, the four fundamental subspaces.
